Definition / Scope Note: Author (1951-1982). Born Busan during Korean War. Not singular narrator but dispersed across Diseuse and multiple women's voice.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Author (1951-1982). Born Busan during Korean War. Not singular narrator but dispersed across Diseuse and multiple women's voices. 'Half-revived, half-buried' authorial presence (Cheng 1998). NOTE: birthdate 1951-03-04 per Wikidata Q7782868 ? verify against BAMPFA archive; earlier research context cited 1952.

Definition / Scope Note: Korean independence activist (1902-1920). Arrested during March 1st Movement, died in Seodaemun Prison age 17.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Korean independence activist (1902-1920). Arrested during March 1st Movement, died in Seodaemun Prison age 17. Central figure in 'exchangeable identity' strategy: 'Her identity... exchangeable with any other heroine in history.' (p.30)

Definition / Scope Note: French martyr (1412-1431). Postcolonial parallel to Yu Gwan-sun: both young women martyred by imperial powers.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: French martyr (1412-1431). Postcolonial parallel to Yu Gwan-sun: both young women martyred by imperial powers. Incantatory invocation p.28: 'She calls the name Jeanne d'Arc three times.' Also appears through Th?r?se's performance and Falconetti's portrayal.

Definition / Scope Note: Carmelite nun (1873-1897). Author of Story of a Soul. Shares name 'Theresa' with Cha (Catholic baptismal name from Sacred Heart Convent). Performs as Joan of Arc in 1895 play.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Carmelite nun (1873-1897). Author of Story of a Soul. Shares name 'Theresa' with Cha (Catholic baptismal name from Sacred Heart Convent). Performs as Joan of Arc in 1895 play. Right-page narrative in ERATO split-screen structure.

Definition / Scope Note: Last Empress of Korea (1851-1895).
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Last Empress of Korea (1851-1895). Assassination date deliberately altered to 1919 in text ? intentional temporal collapse to show colonial violence as recurring structure, not sequential events.

Definition / Scope Note: French actress (1892-1946). Portrays Joan of Arc in Dreyer's silent film La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928).
internal_Definition / Scope Note: French actress (1892-1946). Portrays Joan of Arc in Dreyer's silent film La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928). Silent woman in silent medium ? visual signifier of foreclosed speech throughout ERATO.

Definition / Scope Note: Cha's mother (b.1922 Yongjing, Manchuria). Triple-language speaker under colonial rule: Korean forbidden, Japanese enforced, Chinese ambient. Her experience of linguistic displacement under colonial rule is a central narrative thread in the text.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Cha's mother (b.1922 Yongjing, Manchuria). Triple-language speaker under colonial rule: Korean forbidden, Japanese enforced, Chinese ambient. Embodies intergenerational translational violence. Fictional letter form in CALLIOPE. Portrait p.44 also used in Cha's 1977 video Chronology.

Definition / Scope Note: Cha's father. Calligrapher. His brush calligraphy 女男, 父母 placed at center of pages.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Cha's father. Calligrapher. His brush calligraphy 女男 (pp.26-27), 父母 (pp.54-55) placed at center of pages. Daoist cosmological concepts in TERPSICHORE (p.154). Cantonese pronunciation transcription in POLYMNIA (p.173).

Definition / Scope Note: Cha's older brother. Participated in April 19 Revolution demonstrations. His political activity is referenced in the text as a catalyst for the family's subsequent exile to the United States.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Cha's older brother. Participated in April 19 Revolution demonstrations. Tutor's warning: 'they are killing any student in uniform' (p.84). Family's subsequent exile to US motivated by his political activity. 'De.Mo' syllabic split = democracy decomposed.

Definition / Scope Note: French: female monologue performer. Cha's textual shaman who empties self to channel 9 Muses.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: French: female monologue performer. Cha's textual shaman who empties self to channel 9 Muses: 'She allows others. In place of her. Admits others to make full.' (p.3). Not fluent speaker but medium of fragments: 'noise, groan, bits torn from words.' Takes on punctuation as bodily condition: 'She would become, herself, demarcations.' (p.4). Structural frame for entire work. NOTE: Treated as distinct entity from Cha ? conflation refused at data level.

Definition / Scope Note: Korean shamanic origin myth: abandoned princess journeys to underworld for healing water to save parents, becomes first mudang (shaman)
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Korean shamanic origin myth: abandoned princess journeys to underworld for healing water to save parents, becomes first mudang (shaman). Cha's version: not abandoned but loved child, sent by mother to well where mysterious woman gives magic medicine. 'Do not look back' motif. Arrives home at dusk ? cure not confirmed.

Definition / Scope Note: Greek goddess of spring and the underworld. Her myth of incomplete return from the underworld serves as a structural reference in the text.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Greek goddess of spring/underworld. Structural frame for ELITERE: incomplete return (pomegranate eaten = permanent bond to loss). 'Let the one who is daughter restore spring with her each appearance from beneath the earth.' (p.133). 'Until.' as grammar of unfinished waiting.

Definition / Scope Note: Greek harvest goddess. Her nine-day search for her daughter is referenced in the text as a figure of waiting and maternal longing.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Greek harvest goddess. Searches 9 days/nights for daughter ? parallel to Novena structure and to mother Huh Hyung Soon's waiting in exile. 'Let the one who is mother who waits nine days and nine nights be found.' (p.133).

Definition / Scope Note: Prophetess who sees truth but is not believed. Appears in the text as a figure of unheard speech.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Prophetess who sees truth but is not believed. Parallel to diseuse de bonne aventure (fortune-teller). Both speak truth that existing power structures refuse to hear. Connected to Spivak's 'Can the Subaltern Speak?'

Definition / Scope Note: Fictional character from Carl Theodor Dreyer's film Gertrud (1964). Referenced in the text through the film's narrative of an unhappy marriage.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Fictional character from Dreyer's film Gertrud (1964). Unhappy wife betrayed by husband. Left-page narrative in ERATO's split-screen structure. Her secular suffering mirrors Th?r?se's sacred suffering on facing page. NOTE: fictional character ? ontological class review pending (FRBRoo F38_Character may be more precise than Person).

Definition / Scope Note: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, postcolonial theorist. Best known for 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988), which examines the representational limits of Western intellectual frameworks in relation to colonized subjects.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988). Representational crisis: Vertreten (political proxy) vs Darstellen (portrayal). Framework for Diseuse's mediation and translational-violence concept.

Definition / Scope Note: Hortense Spillers, Black feminist theorist. Best known for 'Mama's Baby, Papa's Maybe: An American Grammar Book' (1987), which theorizes the distinction between flesh and body under conditions of slavery and colonial violence.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Mama's Baby, Papa's Maybe: An American Grammar Book' (1987). flesh/body distinction: enslaved women as 'female but not woman,' reduced to 'zero degree of social conceptualisation.' Ungendering concept. Primary theoretical source for dict:concept/ungendering ? applied to URANIA's blood/ink transformation (pp.64-65).

Definition / Scope Note: María Lugones, decolonial feminist philosopher. Key works include 'Coloniality of Gender' (2007) and 'Toward a Decolonial Feminism' (2010), which argue that gender itself is a colonial imposition and theorize active subjectivity within decolonial practice.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Coloniality of Gender' (2007); 'Toward a Decolonial Feminism' (2010). Gender itself as colonial introduction. Fractured Locus: active subjectivity between colonial designation and communal memory. Framework for shamanic mediation and cyclical time concepts.

Definition / Scope Note: Korean independence uprising against Japanese colonial rule, March 1, 1919. A foundational moment of anti-colonial resistance, referenced in the text through the figure of Yu Gwan-sun.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1919 Korean independence uprising against Japanese colonial rule. Yu Gwan-sun's participation and martyrdom. Temporal anchor: other events (1960, 1980) are 'recurrences' of this foundational structure of colonial violence.

Definition / Scope Note: Student-led uprising against the Syngman Rhee government, April 19, 1960. Referenced in the text in connection with the Cha family's experience of political upheaval in Korea.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1960 student uprising against Syngman Rhee. Brother's participation. 'De.Mo' (p.84): syllabic decomposition of Democracy as empty signifier. 'Dear Mother, 4.19. Four Nineteen... eighteen years later' (p.83).

Definition / Scope Note: Korean War (1950?1953). Theresa Hak Kyung Cha was born during the war in Busan, where her family had taken refuge. Referenced in the text as part of the family's history of displacement.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1950-1953. Mother's Busan refuge. Cha born 1951 during war ? birth itself as product of displacement. 'It is not 6.25. Six twenty five. June 25th 1950. Not today. Not this day.' (p.83). Negation as temporal invocation.

Definition / Scope Note: Pro-democracy uprising in Gwangju, South Korea, May 1980, brutally suppressed by military forces. Cha visited Korea shortly after and witnessed the aftermath. Referenced in the text as a moment of political crisis and historical repetition.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1980 pro-democracy movement brutally suppressed. Cha (age 29) returned to Korea, witnessed aftermath. 'Nothing has changed, we are at a standstill.' (p.87). Third iteration of national self-division after 1919, 1960.

Definition / Scope Note: Japanese colonial rule of Korea (1910?1945). The colonial language policy ? forbidding Korean while enforcing Japanese ? forms a central historical context for the text's engagement with linguistic displacement and intergenerational loss.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1910-1945. Mother's language prohibition: 'They say you spoke in tongue forbidden' (p.45). Yu Gwan-sun's imprisonment and death. Structural context for translational violence across generations.

Definition / Scope Note: State funeral of Emperor Gojong, March 3, 1919. The mass public gathering became a catalyst for the March 1st Movement. Referenced in the text through a contemporary newspaper photograph.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: March 3, 1919. Mass gathering before March 1st Movement. Osaka Asahi Shimbun photograph (p.122) shows Koreans at memorial pavilion, Seoul. Photographic evidence of colonial-era mourning as political assembly.

Definition / Scope Note: The Cha family's emigration from Korea to the United States in 1962. Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, then around age eleven, subsequently settled in San Francisco. Referenced in the text as part of the family's diasporic trajectory.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1962. Mother and brother depart first; Cha (age 11-12) follows to Hawaii, then San Francisco. Defined as 'Exile' not 'Immigration' ? forced departure triggered by brother's political activity. Sacred Heart Convent enrollment follows.

Definition / Scope Note: A critical framework that examines the intersection of colonialism, gender, and knowledge production. Associated with theorists including Spivak and Mohanty, it critiques Western feminist frameworks for their complicity in imperial structures.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Critique of Western imperialism's subjugation of subjects through language and knowledge systems. Mohanty (1984) + Spivak (1988). Upper-level framework for entire Dictee analysis ? all other theoretical concepts operate within this frame.

Definition / Scope Note: Epistemic violence enacted through forced linguistic assimilation across generations. Draws on Spivak's concept of epistemic violence and Fanon's analysis of colonial internalization, applied to the intergenerational linguistic displacement experienced by Cha and her mother under colonial and diasporic conditions.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Intergenerational epistemic violence through forced linguistic assimilation. Mother (Huh Hyung Soon): Japanese enforced → Korean forbidden → Chinese ambient (Manchukuo). Cha: Korean suppressed → English enforced → French acquired (Sacred Heart). Spivak's epistemic violence materialized across two generations. Synthesis of Spivak (1988) + Fanon, Black Skin White Masks (1952) + Cha's text.

Definition / Scope Note: A researcher-developed interpretive concept describing the authorial strategy in Dictee whereby the speaker empties the self to channel the voices of absent or silenced women. The term draws an analogy with shamanic mediation as a structural model, though it is not a term used in Cha's text itself.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: A researcher-developed interpretive concept describing the authorial strategy in Dictee whereby the speaker empties the self to channel the voices of absent or silenced women. The term draws an analogy with shamanic mediation as a structural model, though it is not a term used in Cha's text itself. Evidence type: Modeling.

Definition / Scope Note: Term developed by Mar?a Lugones (2010) to describe the tension between colonial designation and active subjectivity within communal memory. Refers to the space of agency available to those positioned outside dominant social categories.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Her identity... is exchangeable with any other heroine in history, their names, dates, actions which require not definition in their deviation to generosity and self-sacrifice.' (p.30). Lugones (2010): tension between colonial designation as 'non-human' and active subjectivity within communal memory. NOT erasure of individuality but refusal of singular hero narrative.

Definition / Scope Note: A non-linear conception of time in which historical events recur as structural repetitions rather than sequential causes and effects. Draws on Lugones (2010). Applied in this dataset to the recurring pattern of colonial violence across different historical moments.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Dead time. Hollow depression interred... resistant to memory. Waits.' (p.123). Time buried underground, requiring excavation by diseuse's invocation. Connected to Persephone in underworld. 'Until.' ? permanent incompletion. Theoretical basis: Lugones (2010) [primary]; Kusch (tr.2010, orig.1978) via Lugones ? Andean context, NOT directly applied to Korean text.

Definition / Scope Note: Term developed by Hortense Spillers (1987) to describe the exclusion of enslaved and colonized women from normative gender categories entirely. Distinct from gender nonconformity: ungendering refers to a structural violence rather than a chosen identity position.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Spillers (1987): exclusion from gender categories entirely under colonial/slave violence. Enslaved women as 'female but not woman' ? reduced to 'zero degree of social conceptualisation.' Applied to URANIA chapter: 'Sang. Encre.' (Blood. Ink.) ? Cha's body treated as flesh (살덩어리) under medical/colonial gaze, not as gendered subject. Blood extraction (forced, external) → transformation into ink (self-determined) marks transition from ungendering to re-gendering.

Definition / Scope Note: The condition of displacement and longing for return that cannot be fully realized. Draws primarily on Avtar Brah's concept of 'homing desire' (1996), which distinguishes between the mythologized idea of home and the possibility of literal return. Applied to multi-generational displacement across Manchuria, Korea, and the United States.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Brah, Cartographies of Diaspora (1996) [primary]: 'homing desire' ? diaspora space as mythologized, not literal, return. Cha returns to Korea 1980 but witnesses Gwangju; Bari returns with medicine but cure unconfirmed. 'Until.' as grammar of unfinished waiting. Diaspora as structural incompletion. Clifford, 'Diasporas' (1994) [secondary ? heritage/boundary frame, distinct from Brah]. Multi-displacement: Manchuria → Korea → Hawaii → US mainland.

Definition / Scope Note: The remainder that resists full transfer between languages. In Dictee, untranslatability works as a textual strategy rather than a failure: French and English are set on facing pages without equivalence, so that homophones such as cygnes/signes and tense distinctions such as the imperfect j'écoutais against the simple past "I heard" leave a political residue that neither language can absorb. Distinct from dict:concept/translational-violence, which names the loss imposed by colonial language policy; untranslatability names what the text withholds in response. Draws on Emily Apter, Against World Literature: On the Politics of Untranslatability (2013), and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, "The Politics of Translation" (1993).
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Theoretical basis: Apter, Against World Literature: On the Politics of Untranslatability (2013), which theorizes untranslatability as a resource for resisting the smooth circulation of world literature; and Spivak, "The Politics of Translation" (1993), which treats translation as an ethical and political act rather than a neutral transfer. In Dictee, the bilingual poem in URANIA places French and English on facing pages, and the gap between them is deliberately left open. The French homophones cygnes (swans) and signes (signs) cannot be carried into English as a pair, and the imperfect j'écoutais (an ongoing, active listening) is flattened by the English simple past "I heard" (a completed, passive receipt). Each language keeps a remainder that the other cannot hold, and the text refuses to resolve this for the Western reader. Related to dict:concept/translational-violence through the relation translational-violence prefigures untranslatability: the imposed loss of language comes first, and the text's refusal to translate answers it. Evidence type is Modeling because the term does not appear in Cha's text and the concept is applied through an external theoretical frame. Page references to be confirmed: the bilingual poem is at pp. 66–73, but the location of the cygnes/signes and j'écoutais examples should be checked against the 1982 edition.

Each Muse no longer represents a single genre but an unstable intersection of colonial history, martyrdom, and shamanism. THALIA (Comedy) opens with MELPOMENE (Tragedy) fresco ? genre expectation deliberately violated.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Traditional Muses reclaimed as active channels for silenced women across colonial and gendered histories. Each Muse no longer represents a single genre but an unstable intersection of colonial history, martyrdom, and shamanism. THALIA (Comedy) opens with MELPOMENE (Tragedy) fresco ? genre expectation deliberately violated.

Definition / Scope Note: Acupuncture meridian chart from the Chinese medical tradition, included in the text as a visual document. Presents speech and emotion as physiological processes located in specific organs of the body.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Ming dynasty (1341) Shisijing Fahui / Han dynasty Nanjing. Speech as physiological process. Tunstall: 'grief is located in the lungs' in Eastern medicine. Paired with vocal anatomy diagram ? two knowledge systems approaching the same question.

Definition / Scope Note: Western anatomical diagram of the speech organs, included in the text as a visual document. Appears alongside an Eastern meridian chart, juxtaposing two distinct knowledge systems for understanding how the body produces speech.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Western anatomical cross-section of speech organs. Materialization of speech as bodily labor. Juxtaposed with Eastern meridian chart: two knowledge systems approaching the same question (how does the body produce speech?).

Definition / Scope Note: Photograph of Yu Gwan-sun, taken as a Japanese police record card photograph in 1919. Reproduced in the text as a memorial image. Yu Gwan-sun was a Korean independence activist who died in colonial detention.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1919 Japanese police record card photograph. Colonial documentation repurposed as memorial icon. Also appears enlarged from group photo on back cover ? Yu stands at right of back row (Ewha Hakdang students).

Definition / Scope Note: Photograph of Huh Hyung Soon, Cha's mother, taken circa 1940 at approximately age eighteen. Reproduced in the text as an opening image. The same photograph also appears in Cha's 1977 video work Chronology.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Circa 1940 photograph, age ~18. Also used in Cha's 1977 video Chronology ? recurring maternal image across works. Placed at chapter opening as visual anchor for mother's diasporic narrative.

Definition / Scope Note: Photograph published in the French magazine La vie illustrée in 1904, depicting a Korean execution during the Russo-Japanese War. Documents colonial violence through the medium of imperial press photography.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1904 photograph from French magazine La vie illustr?e, showing Korean execution during Russo-Japanese War. Colonial violence documented and consumed by imperial media.

Definition / Scope Note: Map of the Korean peninsula showing the division line between North and South Korea. Reproduced in the text as a visual document of national division.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Korea with division line drawn across center. Visual evidence opening MELPOMENE chapter. 'She' = personification of divided peninsula. 'SHE opposes Her. SHE against her.' (p.87).

prefLabel (en): Thérèse as Joan of Arc Photo
Definition / Scope Note: Photograph taken in 1895 of Saint Th?r?se of Lisieux costumed as Joan of Arc in a play she performed for her sister. Reproduced in the text as a document of performative identity.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1895 photograph: Saint Th?r?se costumed as Joan of Arc in play written for her sister. Identity layering: saint performs as martyr. Entry point for name chain: Cha(Theresa) → Th?r?se → Joan → Falconetti → Gertrud.

prefLabel (en): Dreyer Joan of Arc Film Still
Definition / Scope Note: Film still from Carl Theodor Dreyer's La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928), showing Renée Jeanne Falconetti in close-up as Joan of Arc. Reproduced in the text as a visual document of silenced speech.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Still from La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928). Falconetti's face in close-up. Silent woman in silent film ? foreclosed speech visualized. Chapter's final image.

Definition / Scope Note: Hand stencil painting from El Castillo cave, Spain, estimated at approximately 27,000 years old. One of the earliest known examples of human mark-making. Reproduced in the text as a visual document.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: ~27,000-year-old hand stencil, Spain. Part of Cha's ongoing project on 'representation of hands in Western painting' (Lee-Lenfield). Primordial mark-making. Connected to THALIA's 'Scratch. Marking. Uncontainable.' (p.150).

Definition / Scope Note: Photograph published in the Osaka Asahi Shimbun on March 3, 1919, showing Koreans gathered at a memorial pavilion in Seoul following Emperor Gojong's state funeral. Reproduced in the text as a document of colonial-era public mourning.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: March 3, 1919 Japanese newspaper. Koreans gathered at memorial pavilion, Seoul, after Emperor Gojong's funeral. Colonial documentation as inadvertent archive of resistance. Facing page: 'Dead time' text.

Definition / Scope Note: Roman fresco depicting Melpomene, the Muse of Tragedy, removing a smiling mask to reveal an unsmiling face beneath. Housed at the Getty Museum. Reproduced in the text as a visual opening to a chapter structured around comedy.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Fresco of Melpomene (Tragedy) removing smiling mask to reveal unsmiling face. Comedy chapter (THALIA) opens with Tragedy's image ? genre expectation deliberately violated. Key evidence for dict:concept/muse-subversion.

Definition / Scope Note: Photograph by Francis Frith (1857) of Egyptian ruins along the Nile. Reproduced in the text as a visual document of ancient civilization and temporal depth.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: 1857 Francis Frith photograph of Egyptian ruins along Nile. Ancient civilization as temporal depth ? extends temporal stratigraphy beyond cave hand (27,000 years). NOTE: relationship to other concepts/objects not yet instantiated in File 5.

Definition / Scope Note: Brush calligraphy by Cha Hyung Sang (Cha's father) rendering the characters 女男 (Woman-Man). The sequence reverses the conventional Korean order of 男女 (Man-Woman). Reproduced in the text as a visual document.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Cha Hyung Sang's brush calligraphy 女男 (Woman-Man) centered on pp.26-27. Gendered order reversed from conventional Korean 男女. Father's hand inscribes alternative gender grammar ? connected to dict:concept/ungendering (subversion of colonial gender order).

Definition / Scope Note: Brush calligraphy by Cha Hyung Sang (Cha's father) rendering the characters 父母 (Father-Mother). Reproduced in the text as a visual document within a chapter centered on the mother's narrative.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Cha Hyung Sang's brush calligraphy 父母 (Father-Mother) centered on pp.54-55. Parental dyad as visual anchor in mother's narrative chapter.

Definition / Scope Note: Brush calligraphy by Cha Hyung Sang (Cha's father) rendering ten Daoist cosmological concepts including Taiji, written in Chinese characters. Reproduced in the text as a visual document of cosmological thought.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Ten Daoist cosmic concepts including Taiji. Written in Chinese characters (p.154), Cantonese pronunciation transcribed in POLYMNIA (p.173). Cosmological framework for cyclical structure.

Definition / Scope Note: Pages of English cursive handwriting with visible deletions and line breaks, reproduced in the text as a visual document. Makes visible the process of composition and revision as material labor.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: English cursive handwriting with visible deletions, line breaks. Editorial process made visible ? composition as labor, not finished product. Materiality of writing exposed.

Definition / Scope Note: Korean folk song (봉선화) about separation from family and homeland, embedded in the text without translation. The song's untranslated presence enacts a form of linguistic and cultural resistance.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Korean folk song about separation from family and lost homeland. Embedded untranslated within English text ? translational resistance through song. Connects to dict:concept/untranslatability.

Definition / Scope Note: A dictation exercise in which punctuation marks ? period, comma, open quotation marks ? are written out as words rather than rendered as symbols. Reproduced in the text as a document of language's regulatory function made visible through instruction.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Period', 'Comma', 'Open quotation marks' written as words rather than symbols in dictation exercise. Language's regulatory infrastructure made visible. Diseuse 'would take on their punctuation... become, herself, demarcations.' (p.4). Connects to dict:rel/embodiesPunctuation.

Definition / Scope Note: Independent publisher, New York. Founded by Reese Williams. Cha worked as editor. Published Dictee (1982) and Apparatus (1981). Letterpress printing.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Independent publisher, New York. Founded by Reese Williams. Cha worked as editor. Published Dictee (1982) and Apparatus (1981). Letterpress printing.

Definition / Scope Note: Published 2001 reprint/third edition of Dictee with BAMPFA.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Published 2001 reprint/third edition of Dictee with BAMPFA. Returned book to print after 19 years out of print.

Definition / Scope Note: UC Berkeley. Houses Cha's estate and archives. Rights holder for Dictee. Collaborated with UC Press on 2001 reprint.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: UC Berkeley. Houses Cha's estate and archives. Rights holder for Dictee. Collaborated with UC Press on 2001 reprint.

Definition / Scope Note: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Dictee. New York: Tanam Press, 1982. 179 pp. Artists' book structured around nine chapters named after the Greek Muses, preceded by a prologue centered on the figure of the diseuse (female monologue performer). The work draws on autobiography, history, film, and religious text across multiple languages including Korean, English, French, and Latin.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Target work. 1982 Tanam Press. 179pp. Artists' book. 9 chapters structured by Greek Muses + DISEUSE prologue.

Definition / Scope Note: The diasporic condition of the author and her family after their emigration to the United States in 1962. In Dictee it appears as the experience of speaking from outside the homeland: the letter to the mother dated "eighteen years later" and the account of a return that is also a displacement. The heading names the position from which the work is written.

The work's critical appropriation of a male-centered literary tradition. Dictee borrows the nine Muses, traditionally passive sources of inspiration for male poets, and turns them into frames through which silenced women speak, mediated by the Diseuse (p. 3). Women omitted from official history (Yu Gwan-sun, the author's mother, Thérèse of Lisieux) become its speaking subjects.

The historical frame of Japanese colonial rule that structures the first chapters of Dictee. It appears in the figure of Yu Gwan-sun and the 1919 independence movement and in the enforced loss of the Korean language experienced by the author's mother: "They say you spoke in tongue forbidden."

A Catholic devotion of prayer repeated over nine days. Dictee names it directly in its prologue: "NOVENA: NINE EACH. THE RECITATION OR PRAYER AND PRACTICING OF DEVOTIONS DURING A NINE DAY PERIOD / And it begins" (p. 19). The work frames its nine chapters, each placed under a Muse, as such a sequence of invocations.
internal_Definition / Scope Note: Direct Term: the word and its definition appear in the text (p. 19). Used here not as the general devotional practice but as the structural principle of the work, linking the nine Muses to Demeter's nine days and nights of searching (p. 133).

Definition / Scope Note: The work's own name for time that has stopped and been buried: "Dead time. Hollow depression interred invalid / to resurgence, resistant to memory. Waits." (ELITERE). Time here is not a line that passes but a site to be excavated, which the Diseuse is called upon to break open.
Chapter(s): Direct Term: the phrase appears in the text (p. 123). Textual source for the researcher's Modeling concept dict:concept/cyclical-time, linked by skos:broader. The same passage opens Jennifer Kwon Dobbs, "Diseuse in a Dead Time," Evergreen Review.
